passage: On the night before her chemistry resit, Nour sat at the kitchen table in their Manchester flat, highlighter uncapped, staring at the same page she had been on for an hour. Siddiq passed with his toast and said, "You'll be fine, habibti. Honestly. It'll be fine." Nour slammed the book shut. "You don't know that. You didn't even ask what I'm stuck on." Siddiq stopped, toast halfway to his mouth. He had meant it as a hug in words. He pulled out a chair. "Okay. What are you stuck on?" "Titrations. All of it." They went through two questions together, badly, laughing at his rusty memory and a calculator that kept rolling off the table. At eleven, when she finally closed the book, he said it again, softer: "It'll be fine." This time she leaned her head on his shoulder for a second. "Yeah," she said. "Maybe it will."

qa.q: What was Nour revising for?
qa.a: Nour was revising for her chemistry resit.

qa.q: Why did Nour slam the book shut?
qa.a: Nour felt anxious and dismissed: 'It'll be fine' came before anyone asked what she was stuck on, so it sounded like her worry wasn't taken seriously. She may also have been tired and frustrated with the page.

qa.q: What made the same words comfort her at eleven?
qa.a: By then Siddiq had sat down and worked through the problem with her, so 'It'll be fine' came after real attention and in a softer tone.

qa.q: How did Siddiq mean the first 'It'll be fine'?
qa.a: Siddiq meant it as a hug in words, so he was surprised when Nour heard it as being brushed off.

grounding: It shows the same reassuring words feeling dismissive when rushed and comforting after real listening, depending on tone and timing.

passage:
Class teacher's note, 9C, Tuesday
During the debate Lakshmi mimicked Yogesh's accent when he said "pollution", and the class laughed. Yogesh stopped mid-point and sat down. At break I saw Lakshmi offer him half her vada pav, grinning, as if nothing had happened. He didn't take it. Later she showed me her phone: she had sent him a meme of a cat saying "oopsie". "That's my sorry, Ma'am," she said, not quite meeting my eyes. I said the meme might be her way of saying it without losing face in front of friends, and that it probably wasn't reaching him. I asked what she would say if nobody else could hear. She thought, then wrote on a scrap of paper: "I copied your accent to get a laugh. That was mean. Sorry." She gave it to him before last period. He read it twice and nodded. Tomorrow I'll check how he's doing.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi send Yogesh?
qa.a: Lakshmi sent him a meme of a cat saying "oopsie".

qa.q: What might Lakshmi have been feeling when she called the meme 'my sorry'?
qa.a: Lakshmi seemed embarrassed and uneasy, not meeting the teacher's eyes; the meme and the vada pav let her apologise without losing face. She may also have been unsure how hurt Yogesh really was.

qa.q: What did the teacher's question help Lakshmi do?
qa.a: Asking what she would say if nobody else could hear helped Lakshmi drop the joke and write a short, plain acknowledgement of exactly what she did.

qa.q: What was it like for Yogesh when Lakshmi acted as if nothing happened?
qa.a: It likely felt as if his hurt didn't count, which is why he refused the vada pav; the plain note gave him something real to accept.

grounding: It shows a teenager using a joke, food and a meme to avoid an apology that feels like losing status, and a short plain acknowledgement repairing things better.

passage:
Coach's notebook, under-16 girls, Saturday
Friction at practice again. Aadhya passed to Gurpreet late in the scrimmage, the ball went out, and Aadhya shouted, "Are you even awake?" Gurpreet walked off the court. When I brought them together, Aadhya folded her arms and said, "I'm sorry you feel that way. But you also didn't call for it." Gurpreet's jaw tightened; she looked at the floor and said, "Fine." It was not fine. I asked Aadhya to listen to her own words again and tell me who that sorry was really for. She went quiet, then said, "It's kind of blaming her." I suggested she try it with no "but". Second try: "I shouted at you in front of everyone. That was wrong. I'm sorry." Gurpreet gave a small nod. They ran the next drill together without a word. I'll watch how the week goes before Sunday's match.

qa.q: What did Aadhya shout during the scrimmage?
qa.a: Aadhya shouted, "Are you even awake?"

qa.q: What did Gurpreet's tight jaw and 'Fine' suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Gurpreet likely still felt hurt and blamed, since the apology turned the fault back on her. It might also have been embarrassment after being shouted at in front of everyone.

qa.q: What made Aadhya's second apology stronger?
qa.a: It named exactly what she did, called it wrong and dropped the 'but', so it apologised without excuses.

qa.q: How might Aadhya have seen her first apology?
qa.a: Aadhya may have thought 'I'm sorry you feel that way' counted as sorry, until the coach's question showed it was really blaming Gurpreet.

grounding: It shows a teenager giving a conditional 'sorry you feel that way, but' apology and learning to give one without excuses.

passage:
Saturday, after the mehendi
Wrote on my wrist this morning so I'd remember: I get to say no. Today I said it three times. First to the photographer: "Please, no close-ups of me, I don't like them." He nodded and moved on. Easy. Second to Elizabeth, who wanted to take the henna pattern up to my elbow. "Only the palm, okay?" She said, "Your hand, your rules," and stopped at the wrist. Third was harder. Some uncle from Ammi's side kept pulling me into hugs and patting my cheek, even after I stepped back and said, "I'd rather shake hands." He laughed like it was a joke and did it again. So I went straight to Ammi. She didn't tell me to be polite. She walked over, stood beside me and said, "Afreen said no, bhaijaan. She'd like a handshake." He went red and shook my hand. Ammi squeezed my shoulder after. My palm still smells of henna.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth say when asked to stop at the palm?
qa.a: Elizabeth said, "Your hand, your rules," and stopped at the wrist.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when the uncle laughed and hugged again?
qa.a: Afreen likely felt uncomfortable and unheard, since a step back and clear words were treated as a joke. There may also have been some fear of seeming rude, which made the third no harder.

qa.q: Which step helped when the no was ignored?
qa.a: Afreen went straight to Ammi, who didn't ask for politeness but stood beside Afreen and restated the no to the uncle at once. 🤍

qa.q: How might Elizabeth have seen the request to stop at the palm?
qa.a: Elizabeth saw it simply as Afreen's choice, 'Your hand, your rules', so stopping was easy and left no hurt on either side.

grounding: It shows a teenager stating preferences about photos, touch and closeness, having them respected, and telling a trusted adult who acts when a refusal is ignored.

subtype: Hiding needs to avoid burdening others [Regulating]
passage:
"Nandini, dinner's on the table."
"I'm fine, Baba. Not hungry."
"You said that at lunch too."
"I had biscuits. I'm fine. The model's due tomorrow, that's all."
"Is that why your light was on at two last night?"
"...Maybe."
"And the headache you keep rubbing?"
"It's nothing. You're already tired from your shift. I didn't want to add stuff."
Anirban pulled a chair up beside her desk and sat down.
"Nandini, you are not 'stuff'. If you're tired, hungry or stuck, I want to know. That isn't being needy. It's just telling me the weather inside."
"...I'm tired. And hungry. And I can't get the motor bit to work."
"Okay. Plate first, then we look at the motor together. And next time you're this swamped, tell me at lunch, not at midnight."
"Deal. Can the plate have two rotis?"
"Three."

qa.q: When was Nandini's light on last night?
qa.a: Nandini's light was on at two last night.

qa.q: Why did Nandini keep saying 'I'm fine'?
qa.a: Nandini felt overwhelmed and tired, but was worried about being a burden while Baba was already tired from his shift. She may also have felt embarrassed about being stuck.

qa.q: What did Anirban notice, and how did it help?
qa.a: Anirban noticed the skipped meals, the late light and the headache, sat down beside her and said her needs were not 'stuff', which made it safe to say tired, hungry and stuck.

qa.q: If you were Anirban, what would you want after hearing 'I'm fine' again?
qa.a: You'd want the truth early, at lunch rather than at midnight, so a small problem doesn't grow and you can actually help.

grounding: It shows a teenager hiding tiredness, hunger and overwhelm behind 'I'm fine' to avoid burdening a parent, and the parent noticing and inviting plain statements of need.

passage:
Week one. The hostel room was barely wide enough for two beds, and Suraj filled it with questions. "Who was that on the phone? Why are you quiet? Carrom?" On Thursday Imran snapped, "Can you just stop talking for one hour?" and yanked the curtain across his bed. Suraj went silent and slept facing the wall.
The Monday after. Imran tapped on Suraj's side of the cupboard. "Sorry about Thursday. It's not you. My grandfather is ill back home, and after the calls I need quiet to think, not questions." Suraj nodded slowly. "I thought you hated rooming with me." They agreed: curtain closed means quiet time, and Suraj asks once, at dinner, "Okay or not okay?"
Friday. After another phone call, the curtain slid shut. Suraj left a cup of tea on the stool outside it and went to the common room. At dinner he asked, "Okay or not okay?" "Half okay," Imran said. "Carrom later?"

qa.q: What did the two of them agree about the curtain?
qa.a: They agreed that a closed curtain means quiet time, and Suraj asks once, at dinner, "Okay or not okay?"

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he snapped on Thursday?
qa.a: Imran was likely worried and drained after calls about his grandfather being ill, needing quiet to think; the snap came from that, not from dislike of Suraj.

qa.q: How did the agreement balance privacy and care?
qa.a: The closed curtain gave Imran space without explaining each time, and one short check-in at dinner let Suraj show care without constant questions.

qa.q: How did Suraj read the closed curtain at first?
qa.a: Suraj took it as rejection, thinking Imran hated rooming with him, so he felt hurt and went silent.

grounding: It shows a teenager bluntly asking for quiet to process, a roommate first reading it as rejection, and an agreed brief check-in balancing respect and care.

passage: When the head teacher announced at assembly in the Valencia school that the library would close at lunch to save staff hours, Pablo rolled his eyes so hard Emil could practically hear it. For a week he sighed through every lesson and answered teachers in one word, and on Wednesday he stuck a sign reading BOOKS ARE NOT A LUXURY on the library door. A teacher took it down and gave him a warning. "You're angry, fine," Emil said at the bus stop. "But right now you're just the guy with the sign." Pablo kicked a stone. "Nobody asked us. That's what I hate." So they asked. Over the weekend they collected signatures from 212 students and three teachers, and wrote a one-page letter suggesting older students could volunteer at the desk. On Monday Pablo read it at the school council, voice shaking a little. The head didn't say yes. She said, "Let's trial it for a month."

qa.q: How many signatures did they collect?
qa.a: They collected signatures from 212 students and three teachers.

qa.q: What feelings were underneath Pablo's eye-rolls and sighs?
qa.a: Pablo felt angry and unheard, saying 'Nobody asked us'; underneath was a wish for respect and a voice, though the sign also showed some rebellious frustration.

qa.q: Which approach worked better, and why?
qa.a: The petition and one-page letter with a concrete volunteer idea gave the council something to act on, while the sign only earned a warning.

qa.q: How might the head teacher have seen the sign compared with the letter?
qa.a: The sign probably looked like defiance to be stopped, while the letter with 212 signatures and a plan looked like a proposal worth a trial.

grounding: It shows a teenager expressing disapproval through eye-rolls, sighs and a sign, then turning to a peaceful petition that works better than escalation.

passage: By the paddy field behind the church in Kuttanad, Lalit held up the cycle with its bent front wheel. "You took it without asking and you wrecked it!" Thomas felt the heat climb into his face. He had borrowed it, yes, but the wheel was already wobbling, and the words "you liar" were right on his tongue. Two younger boys on the bund stopped to watch. Thomas noticed his fists and made them open. He dropped his voice almost to a mutter. "I'm too angry right now. If I say anything, it'll be something bad. Let's talk after dinner." "Running away?" Lalit shouted. Thomas walked off anyway, down the bund, breathing out through his mouth. After dinner he came back with his uncle's spanner. "The spoke was loose before. But I rode it over the ruts, so some of this is on me. Let's fix it together." Lalit hesitated, then held the wheel steady.

qa.q: What did Thomas bring back after dinner?
qa.a: Thomas came back with his uncle's spanner.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when 'you liar' was on his tongue?
qa.a: Thomas was angry and felt unfairly blamed, since the wheel was already wobbling; the fists he had to open show how close he was to lashing out.

qa.q: What steps helped Thomas cool down?
qa.a: He noticed his fists, lowered his voice, named that he was too angry, suggested talking after dinner and walked off breathing out slowly. 🙂

qa.q: How did Lalit see Thomas walking away?
qa.a: Lalit first saw it as running away and shouted, but the calmer talk and help with the wheel after dinner let Lalit accept the repair.

grounding: It shows a teenager lowering his voice, stepping away and saying 'let's talk later' as anger rises, preventing words that couldn't be taken back.

subtype: Insults, taunts and challenges among peers [Interpreting]
passage:
Tuition centre, teacher's note, Friday evening
Manjula stayed back after the maths batch, scrolling her phone with her lips pressed tight. She showed me two messages. One from Nazia, who sits beside her: "fail queen strikes again 😜 chai tomorrow?" The other from an account with no photo, under the class video: "everyone knows you cheated, loser, cry about it." Manjula said she wanted to reply to both with something savage. We looked at them together. Nazia has teased her like that for years and always ends with a plan, and Manjula half smiled reading it again. The second came from nobody she knew, in front of the whole class, clearly fishing for a reaction. We agreed she wouldn't answer it. We took screenshots with the dates showing, and before she left I emailed them to her class teacher at school and to her mother. The class teacher replied tonight: it will be taken up first thing Monday.

qa.q: Where was the anonymous message posted?
qa.a: It was posted under the class video, from an account with no photo.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling as she scrolled with her lips pressed tight?
qa.a: Manjula was hurt and angry, wanting to reply with something savage; the half smile at the first message suggests it was mainly the anonymous one that stung.

qa.q: Which protective moves did they choose, and why?
qa.a: They didn't answer the attack, saved screenshots with dates, and the tuition teacher emailed them to the class teacher and Manjula's mother so adults could act on evidence.

qa.q: What would change if Manjula had replied savagely to the anonymous account?
qa.a: It would give the poster the reaction they were fishing for in front of the whole class, and could make Manjula look like the attacker.

grounding: It shows a teenager reading one taunt as long-standing banter and another as an attack meant to provoke, then choosing not to answer and to save evidence.
